```{r register-chunks, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", out.width = "100%",
                      fig.align = "center", message = FALSE, warning = TRUE)
knitr::read_chunk("scripts/texture-gallery.R")
```

```{r gallery-tools, include=FALSE}
```

A texture can be a number, a color, an image, or a computation that combines
other textures. Feed its output into a material input to vary that input over
the surface. The same scalar field can control several inputs: a pale region
can also be rougher, or a dark stripe can also be polished.

This gallery contains **26 renders in ten comparisons**. Each recipe below is
the code used to generate its figure. The supplied images make the vignette
quick to build; the final section explains how to regenerate them.

These are surface-parameter recipes. A stone-like color pattern does not create
stone geometry, and varying roughness does not change the object's silhouette.

# Start with a scalar field

`texture_noise()` produces a scalar between zero and one. It is seeded smooth
value noise, with smaller contributions from successive octaves. Its seed is
independent of the render's sampling seed.

`texture_mix(a, b, weight)` computes `(1 - weight) * a + weight * b`. Its weight
is clamped to `[0, 1]`. The first mix below expands the noise range; using that
result as the next mix's weight makes the patches more distinct.

The left image shows the scalar field through a diffuse grayscale material, so
its brightness also includes lighting and shadows. The middle and right images
reuse that field for a two-color palette. On the right, the gold-colored patches
also have greater roughness.

```{r shared-field, fig.alt="Three spheres showing a grayscale noise mask, the same mask driving blue and gold color, and the same mask also driving roughness."}
```

`grain`, `mask`, `pigment`, and `roughness` are serializable texture descriptions.
They do not contain R callbacks. Scene construction turns their graphs into
native nodes, which evaluate at surface hits.

# Put patterns inside patterns

A checker's two children need not be colors. One child below is another checker.
The third recipe turns a 3D checker into horizontal bands by setting its x and z
coordinate scales to zero, then puts a noise-based palette between those bands.

```{r nested-patterns, fig.alt="A fine checker, a nested checker with coral cells, and a sphere with alternating gold stripes and blue-green noisy bands."}
```

The pattern belongs to the texture; the material describes how it reflects
light. A checker can therefore drive color, roughness, or another mix's weight.

# Stretch and combine noise

Unequal coordinate scales stretch the pattern. Here, a larger y scale creates
closely spaced variation along y. A rotation tilts the pattern in the texture
xy plane. The third material uses a second, broader noise field to blend two
complete **color recipes**.

These suggest wood and stone rather than simulating their physical structure.
All three objects retain exactly the same smooth spherical geometry.

```{r stretched-noise, fig.alt="Three smooth spheres with stretched brown noise, gray stone-like noise, and a broad mixture of the two palettes."}
```

This rotation argument rotates about the texture z axis. It is useful for UV
rotation and for tilting 3D patterns in xy; it is not an arbitrary three-axis
texture transform or a domain-warping system.

# Use orientation as a mask

`texture_direction_mix()` uses the geometric surface normal. Its argument order
follows PBRT: alignment weights **the first input**. This differs from
`texture_mix()`, where a weight of one selects the second input.

With `absolute = TRUE`, the weight is `abs(dot(normal, direction))`. Upward and
downward faces receive the same value. For a deposited-on-top appearance, use
`absolute = FALSE`, which uses `max(0, dot(normal, direction))` instead.

The final recipe multiplies that one-sided orientation mask by noise. It breaks
up the pale region and also increases roughness there. It changes color and
roughness; it does not add a physical layer of dust or snow.

```{r directional, fig.alt="Absolute normal weighting colors both poles, one-sided weighting colors only upper surfaces, and multiplying the upward mask by noise creates irregular pale patches."}
```

The direction is fixed in world space by default. This is **not a facing-ratio or
Fresnel texture**: moving the camera does not move the mask. Set `space =
"object"` to anchor its direction to the object instead. Bump mapping does not
change this geometric-normal mask.

# Choose where the texture lives

Object coordinates move with the primitive and survive instancing. World
coordinates include the placement of each instance. The two spheres in each
image below are instances of the same source sphere.

The object-space gradient repeats from blue to orange in each sphere. The
world-space gradient spans both placements: the left sphere samples its blue
end and the right sphere its orange end. The gradient clamps at its endpoints;
it does not repeat.

```{r coordinate-spaces, fig.alt="Two pairs of instanced spheres: an object-space gradient repeats in both; a world-space gradient spans the pair."}
```

Each node owns its mapping. Changing an image node's UV offset does not move a
separate roughness node. Mapping applies scale, then rotation about z, then
offset. Negative scales mirror a mapping; zero scales suppress variation along
an axis.

## UV coordinates have their own distortion

A 3D checker evaluates the position of the surface inside a grid of cubes. Its
intersection with a sphere need not look like square tiles. A UV checker instead
uses the sphere's parameterization. Its cells narrow and converge near the poles.

```{r uv-versus-object, fig.alt="A position-based checker on a sphere compared with a UV checker whose cells converge near the poles."}
```

Composing textures does not remove UV seams or stretching. Choose 3D coordinates
for a pattern that should cut through an object, or supply suitable mesh UVs for
a pattern that should follow its surface. UV images use the mapped x and y
coordinates; they are not automatically projected triplanarly.

# Change the finish with a scalar output

The first two spheres keep the same color texture and metallic base. The
roughness bands in the middle image alternate between sharp and broad
reflections. The third sphere shows that the same graph can feed the existing
`microfacet()` material.

```{r roughness-finishes, fig.alt="Gold-colored spheres with constant roughness, alternating polished and rough bands in OpenPBR, and the same roughness graph on a microfacet material."}
```

The numbers are interpreted by the receiving material. `microfacet()` retains
its existing numeric roughness conversion; OpenPBR uses its own model. The same
number is not a promise of identical highlight width across the two shaders.
Within each material, a texture value follows that material's numeric-input
semantics.

## Make glass clearer in one orientation

The checker floor makes refraction easier to see. Both spheres use OpenPBR solid
transmission, constant IOR, and identical geometry. Only roughness changes.

The second sphere is clearest where its geometric normal aligns with a fixed
direction close to the camera's position, and rougher toward the silhouette.
The camera is fixed for this example; moving it would not update the texture's
direction automatically.

```{r glass, fig.alt="Clear glass over a checker floor compared with glass whose roughness increases toward its silhouette."}
```

This is the same kind of parameter operation as PBRT's `directionmix` roughness
texture. PBRT import transforms the declared direction and evaluates its
roughness remapping **after** the texture blend. It does not blend the BSDFs of
two separate glass materials.

# Images can be graph inputs too

The small RGB tile below is generated entirely in R, so the example needs no
downloaded assets. Its channels deliberately contain different patterns.

```{r make-image}
```

```{r source-image, echo=FALSE, out.width="24%", fig.alt="Original RGB tile with concentric rings, a vertical ramp, and diagonal bands in separate channels."}
knitr::include_graphics(tile_file)
```

Extracting its red channel gives a scalar mask that can drive a new palette.
The last sphere uses another image node with its own repeat, rotation, and offset
to control roughness. Changing that mapping leaves the color mapping alone.

```{r image-composition, fig.alt="An RGB image on a metallic sphere, its red channel recolored blue and gold, and that recolored sphere with independently mapped roughness."}
```

Color-to-scalar conversion is explicit. Use `texture_channel(x, "r")`, `"g"`,
`"b"`, `"average"`, or `"luminance"`. A scalar can broadcast to a color, but a
color cannot silently become a roughness value or mixing weight.

For images, `encoding = "auto"` treats scalar maps as linear data and ordinary
LDR color images as sRGB; EXR/HDR defaults to linear. Use an explicit encoding
when the file's contents differ from those assumptions. Decoding happens before
bilinear filtering and mixing. A scalar image averages its RGB channels; it does
not automatically interpret its alpha channel as a mask. The `red_mask` above
uses the red channel **after sRGB decoding**, while `image_roughness` reads the
RGB average as **linear data**.

# Small patterns expose the filtering limit

Procedural patterns currently evaluate a point sample. They have no knowledge
of the pixel's projected footprint. The dense checker below has cells smaller
than a pixel in parts of the image, so the render cannot resolve every cell.

```{r fine-patterns, fig.alt="A coarse checker floor with resolved cells and a much denser checker floor showing subpixel sampling artifacts."}
```

More samples can reduce sampling noise, and rendering larger and downsampling
can help. Neither supplies analytic filtering to the procedural texture. For
stable fine detail, reduce the pattern frequency. Image nodes use bilinear
filtering, but do not yet have mipmapped or anisotropic footprint filtering.

# Supported inputs and limitations

| Material | Inputs that currently accept graphs |
|:--|:--|
| `diffuse()` | `color` |
| `microfacet()` | `color`, `roughness` |
| `openpbr()` | `base_color`, `specular_roughness` |

The examples stay within those inputs. In particular:

- **No graph-driven bump, normal, or displacement.** The apparent grain and
  weathering in the renders do not change the surface normals or silhouette.
  Existing non-graph bump arguments remain available separately.
- **No graph-driven alpha, emission, volume coefficients, or other OpenPBR
  controls yet.** A roughness graph on glass works; a graph for
  `transmission_weight`, `coat_weight`, or `subsurface_color` is not supported.
- **Parameter mixing is not material mixing.** `texture_mix()` produces values
  for one material. There is no public graph-based `mix_material()` operation.
  Blending two roughness values constructs one intermediate distribution, rather
  than a weighted sum of two complete BSDFs.
- **One source per input.** Do not combine a color graph with legacy
  `image_texture`, checker, noise, or gradient arguments for that same color.
  Likewise, choose a roughness graph or `roughness_texture`, not both.
- **Roughness has a numerical floor.** Spatial `microfacet()` roughness uses a
  minimum alpha of `1e-6`; a constant zero roughness selects its existing smooth
  material. OpenPBR has its own reference-model roughness floor. A transmitting
  `microfacet()` color graph requires nonzero roughness.
- **Graph outputs are scalar or color.** Public roughness graphs are scalar;
  there is no public pair of independent u/v roughness graphs or vector-valued
  normal graph. Existing numeric anisotropy controls remain available separately.
  Use the provided constructors rather than arbitrary R callbacks or arithmetic
  operators on the graph objects.
- **Transforms and filtering are bounded.** Mapping supports scale, translation,
  and rotation about texture z. There is no public domain warping, triplanar node,
  time-varying texture node, or procedural footprint antialiasing yet.
- **Sharing does not imply complete memoization.** Shared nodes and decoded
  images avoid duplicate storage, but cross-slot/per-hit expression memoization
  is not implemented. An expensive field used by several inputs may be evaluated
  more than once. Keep graphs proportionate to the visible detail.

Unsupported inputs should not be replaced by guessed alternatives in examples.
For example, this is intentionally an error:

```{r unsupported-slot, error=TRUE}
openpbr(coat_weight = texture_noise())
```

Use a constant `coat_weight` with a supported texture input until that slot gains
graph support.

# Reproduce the gallery

`scripts/texture-gallery.R` contains every recipe above and the small
`texture_panel()` rendering helper. It uses a common studio, fixed exposure and
camera within each comparison, seed `20261002`, and **six rendering cores**.
Images are 420 by 420 pixels, except the wider instancing comparison. Samples are
64 per pixel, or 128 for metal, glass, and image comparisons. No denoising or
bloom is applied.

From the repository root, with this development version of rayrender installed:

```{r regenerate, eval=FALSE}
Sys.setenv(RAYRENDER_REBUILD_TEXTURES = "true")
source("vignettes/scripts/texture-gallery.R", chdir = FALSE)
Sys.unsetenv("RAYRENDER_REBUILD_TEXTURES")
```

The script switches into the vignette directory when run from the repository
root. Set `RAYRENDER_TEXTURE_GROUPS` to a comma-separated set of figure names
(for example, `"glass,image-composition"`) to regenerate selected comparisons
once the gallery exists. Individual renders, labeled comparisons, and per-image
timings are retained under `figures/composable-textures/`.

The material recipes also work without the gallery helper. A minimal standalone
render looks like this:

```{r standalone, eval=FALSE}
library(rayrender)
options(cores = 6L)
n = texture_noise(scale = 5, seed = 7)
surface = openpbr(
  base_color = texture_mix("steelblue", "wheat", n),
  specular_roughness = texture_mix(.05, .6, n)
)
scene = sphere(material = surface) |>
  add_object(generate_ground(depth = -1))
set.seed(20261002)
render_scene(scene, width = 600, height = 600, samples = 64,
  lookfrom = c(3, 1.5, 5), lookat = c(0, 0, 0),
  ambient_light = TRUE, denoise = FALSE, filename = "my-texture.png")
```

To build this document from the existing images, leave
`RAYRENDER_REBUILD_TEXTURES` unset and use `rmarkdown::render()` or the package's
normal vignette build. No gallery path tracing is performed in that mode.
